explanation: Redshift automatically takes periodic snapshots, and also supports on-demand manual snapshots, stored in S3, which can be used to restore a cluster to a prior point in time to recover from data loss or corruption. Spectrum and materialized views are query features, not backup and recovery mechanisms.

stem: After enabling an S3 Lifecycle rule that transitions objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days, a team notices that many small objects, only a few KB each, now cost more in overhead than before the transition, despite the lower per-GB Glacier price. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: S3 Glacier Deep Archive charges no fees regardless of object size, so this cannot happen

Each object transitioned to a Glacier storage class incurs a fixed per-object metadata overhead billed at S3 Standard rates, which can make archiving very small objects cost-inefficient relative to their storage savings
S3 Lifecycle rules cannot be applied to objects smaller than 128 KB
Small objects are automatically deleted instead of transitioned

explanation: S3 Glacier storage classes add a per-object metadata overhead, billed at S3 Standard rates, in addition to the archived data itself, so archiving very small objects can make the overhead outweigh the storage savings; AWS recommends aggregating small objects before archiving. Lifecycle rules do apply to small objects, so that option is false.

stem: A team needs the ability to restore a DynamoDB table to any point in time within the last 35 days after an application bug caused unwanted writes, without needing to manually schedule backups. Which feature should be enabled?

choices.text: DynamoDB on-demand backup only
DynamoDB Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR)
DynamoDB Streams
DynamoDB Global Tables

explanation: Point-in-Time Recovery continuously backs up table data, allowing restoration to any second within the preceding 35 days without needing a manual backup schedule. On-demand backups are full snapshots taken at specific points in time, not continuous, second-level coverage.

stem: A versioning-enabled S3 bucket has a Lifecycle rule that expires the current version of objects after 90 days, but has no rule covering noncurrent versions. What is the consequence of this configuration over time?

choices.text: Expiring the current version automatically deletes all noncurrent versions as well, keeping storage flat

A delete marker is created for the current version after 90 days, but all prior noncurrent versions remain stored indefinitely, so storage costs continue to grow unless a noncurrent version expiration rule is also added
Versioned buckets ignore Lifecycle expiration rules entirely
The bucket automatically disables versioning once the first object expires

explanation: In a versioned bucket, an expiration action on the current version inserts a delete marker rather than truly deleting the underlying data; without a separate rule for noncurrent version expiration, all prior versions persist and continue to accrue storage costs. Lifecycle rules do apply to versioned buckets, and versioning is never automatically disabled by expiration.

stem: A large Redshift fact table is frequently joined to a dimension table on customer_id, and queries commonly filter and aggregate by order_date. Which combination of schema design choices would most improve query performance?

choices.text: Set the sort key to a column never used in WHERE clauses and choose ALL distribution style for the large fact table
Set the distribution key to customer_id to enable collocated joins, and set the sort key to order_date to enable efficient range-restricted scans
Avoid setting any distribution or sort keys so Redshift decides automatically at query time
Set the sort key to customer_id and leave distribution style as EVEN for both tables

explanation: Choosing a distribution key that matches the common join column colocates matching rows on the same node slice, avoiding data redistribution during joins, while a sort key on order_date enables zone-map pruning for range-restricted scans. Applying ALL distribution to a large fact table wastes storage and compute at scale, since ALL distribution is intended for small, frequently joined dimension tables.

stem: When designing tables that will be governed by AWS Lake Formation for a multi-tenant data lake, which practice best supports enforcing column-level security for sensitive fields such as national ID numbers?

choices.text: Store sensitive and non-sensitive columns in the same table with no separation, relying only on application-level filtering
Define the table schema in the Glue Data Catalog with clearly identified sensitive columns, then use Lake Formation column-level permissions or data filters to restrict which principals can view them
Store all sensitive data in a separate AWS account with no catalog entry at all
Encrypt the entire table with a single shared KMS key and grant all users decrypt permission

explanation: Lake Formation enforces fine-grained, column-level and row-level access control on top of the catalog schema, so clearly identifying sensitive columns lets administrators declaratively grant or deny access to specific principals. Relying purely on application-level filtering, or a shared-key grant-all approach, does not provide centrally governed access control.

stem: A DynamoDB table originally designed with a partition key of order_status, a low-cardinality attribute with only four possible values, is now experiencing hot-partition throttling as write volume has grown substantially. What is the most appropriate schema-level fix to address this changed data characteristic?

choices.text: Switch the table's billing mode from on-demand to provisioned to eliminate throttling
Redesign the partition key to use a higher-cardinality attribute, or add a calculated suffix for write sharding, so writes spread across many partitions instead of concentrating on just four values
Add a global secondary index using the same order_status partition key to double the write capacity
Reduce the table's read capacity to free up more write capacity

explanation: A low-cardinality partition key like a four-value status field concentrates traffic onto a small number of physical partitions, causing hot-partition throttling regardless of billing mode; the fix is choosing a higher-cardinality key or applying write sharding to distribute the workload evenly. Changing billing mode or adding a GSI on the same key does not resolve the underlying key-design problem.

stem: A team is migrating an on-premises Oracle data warehouse schema to Amazon Redshift and needs to convert Oracle-specific schema objects, including tables, views, and stored procedures, into a Redshift-compatible schema before migrating the actual data. Which tool is designed for this schema conversion step?

choices.text: AWS Database Migration Service (DMS)
AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT)
AWS Glue DataBrew
AWS DataSync

explanation: AWS SCT automatically converts source database schema objects, such as tables, views, and stored procedures, into syntax compatible with the target engine, flagging objects that require manual conversion. DMS focuses on migrating and replicating the actual data, though it now also offers an integrated schema conversion feature, SCT remains the dedicated standalone schema conversion tool.

stem: A team wants schema conversion and data migration handled within a single managed AWS Database Migration Service project, using DMS's built-in schema conversion capability instead of a separately installed desktop application. Which statement accurately compares this option to using the standalone AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT)?

choices.text: DMS Schema Conversion is a managed, console-integrated feature that performs schema assessment and conversion within DMS, whereas SCT is a separately installed desktop or CLI application; both draw on similar underlying conversion technology
DMS Schema Conversion and SCT are entirely unrelated tools with no shared capability
SCT can migrate live data, while DMS Schema Conversion cannot convert any schema objects
DMS Schema Conversion only supports migrations where the source and target are the same database engine

explanation: AWS DMS Schema Conversion offers a managed, console-integrated experience for schema assessment and conversion, similar in capability to the standalone SCT application but without requiring separate installation. SCT converts schema definitions rather than migrating live data, and DMS Schema Conversion supports heterogeneous engine conversions, not just same-engine migrations.

stem: A data science team needs to trace which raw dataset, processing job, and feature transformations produced a specific trained model version, for auditability. Which capability provides this lineage tracking?

choices.text: Amazon SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking
AWS Glue Data Quality
Amazon Redshift system views
Amazon S3 Inventory

explanation: SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking records the relationships between datasets, processing jobs, training jobs, and model artifacts, creating an auditable graph of how a model was produced. S3 Inventory reports on object-level metadata and does not track ML pipeline lineage.

stem: A governance team wants business users browsing Amazon SageMaker Catalog to see not just a dataset's schema, but also which upstream sources and transformation jobs produced it. What underlying capability supports surfacing this lineage information within the catalog experience?

choices.text: SageMaker Catalog integrates with lineage tracking to surface dataset-to-source relationships alongside business metadata, giving users visibility into data provenance
SageMaker Catalog can only show column names and data types, with no lineage information available
Lineage information must be manually re-entered as free-text notes with no system linkage
Lineage can only be viewed through raw Glue Data Catalog table properties, never through SageMaker Catalog

explanation: SageMaker Catalog, as part of the unified data and AI governance experience, surfaces lineage and provenance information alongside business glossary and technical metadata, helping business users understand where data came from and how it was transformed, rather than showing schema information alone.

stem: A data lake table stored as Parquet in S3 is queried through Athena almost always with a filter on the event_date column, and the table has grown to hundreds of millions of rows. Which design change would most reduce the amount of data scanned, and therefore cost and latency, per query?

choices.text: Partition the S3 data and Glue table by event_date so Athena can prune partitions that do not match the query's date filter
Convert the files from Parquet to uncompressed CSV
Merge all files into a single very large file regardless of date
Add a global secondary index to the S3 bucket

explanation: Partitioning by the commonly filtered column lets Athena skip entire partitions that do not match the WHERE clause, drastically reducing scanned data and cost. Converting to uncompressed CSV would increase the amount of data scanned, and S3 has no concept of a global secondary index, which is a DynamoDB construct.

stem: A Redshift table was created without explicit column encoding, resulting in larger-than-necessary disk usage and slower scan performance. What is the recommended way to improve storage efficiency and query performance for this table?

choices.text: Apply appropriate column compression encodings, for example by using COPY's automatic compression analysis or running ANALYZE COMPRESSION, so each column uses an encoding suited to its data characteristics
Disable compression entirely because Redshift performs better on raw, uncompressed data
Convert the table into a view to avoid storing any data on disk
Increase the cluster's node count without changing the table's encoding

explanation: Redshift stores data in a columnar format and benefits significantly from per-column compression encodings; running ANALYZE COMPRESSION or letting COPY auto-select encodings reduces I/O and improves scan performance. Disabling compression, or simply adding nodes without addressing encoding, wastes storage and does not fix the root inefficiency.

stem: Which statement correctly contrasts the role of a Redshift sort key with a DynamoDB Global Secondary Index (GSI)?

choices.text: A Redshift sort key physically orders data on disk to enable efficient range scans and zone-map pruning within a single table, while a DynamoDB GSI creates a separate, independently provisioned index with a different partition or sort key to support additional query patterns beyond the base table's primary key
Both serve identical purposes; they are the same mechanism with different names across services
A Redshift sort key can be added or changed at query time with no effect on stored data layout, just like a DynamoDB GSI
A DynamoDB GSI physically reorders the base table's items on disk, exactly like a Redshift sort key

explanation: A Redshift sort key determines the physical row ordering within a table to accelerate scans, whereas a DynamoDB GSI is a separate index structure with its own key schema and capacity that enables querying the same data by different attributes. They both aid query efficiency but are structurally very different mechanisms, and neither statement B, C, nor D accurately describes them.

stem: In the context of building a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) application using an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base, what does the vectorization (embedding) step accomplish?

choices.text: It compresses source documents using gzip to reduce S3 storage costs
It converts text chunks into numerical vector representations that capture semantic meaning, enabling similarity search against a vector store
It translates documents from one human language to another before indexing
It automatically removes personally identifiable information from documents

explanation: Vectorization, or embedding, transforms text into dense numerical vectors that capture semantic meaning, which are stored in a vector store such as Amazon OpenSearch Serverless or Aurora with pgvector, allowing a Bedrock knowledge base to perform semantic similarity search at query time. It has nothing to do with compression, translation, or PII redaction.

stem: A team is designing a DynamoDB schema for an e-commerce order system and is deciding between normalizing data, using separate items requiring multiple queries to assemble an order view, versus denormalizing, such as embedding product details within each order item. What is the primary tradeoff of choosing denormalization in DynamoDB?

choices.text: Denormalization has no downsides in DynamoDB and should always be preferred over normalization

Denormalization improves read performance by retrieving all needed data in fewer requests, at the cost of increased storage and the added complexity of keeping duplicated data consistent when the source data changes
Denormalization is not possible in DynamoDB because it automatically enforces third normal form
Denormalization only affects write costs and has no impact on read patterns

explanation: Because DynamoDB lacks joins, denormalizing data needed together reduces the number of requests for common access patterns, improving read latency and throughput, but increases storage usage and requires application logic or a streams-based fan-out to keep duplicated copies consistent when the source changes. DynamoDB does not enforce any relational normal form.

stem: A data engineering team needs to orchestrate a workflow of AWS Glue jobs, EMR steps, and Lambda functions that must run in a specific dependency order, with built-in visual monitoring of each step's state (Running, Succeeded, Failed) in the AWS Management Console, and the team does not want to provision or manage any orchestration infrastructure such as an Apache Airflow environment. Which service best fits this requirement?

choices.text: Amazon MWAA
AWS Step Functions
Amazon EventBridge Scheduler
AWS Glue workflows

explanation: Step Functions is a fully managed, serverless orchestrator with built-in visual state tracking and no environment to provision, unlike MWAA which still requires configuring and scaling an Airflow environment. EventBridge Scheduler only invokes targets on a schedule with no branching or visual execution tracking, and Glue workflows only orchestrate Glue-native crawlers/jobs/triggers rather than arbitrary EMR steps and Lambda together.

stem: Tasks in an Amazon MWAA environment are remaining in the queued state for a long time before executing, even though the DAG code has no bugs and the scheduler shows no errors. Which configuration change is most likely to resolve this?

choices.text: Increase the MWAA environment class or the maximum worker count
Decrease the DAG's schedule_interval
Enable versioning on the MWAA environment's S3 bucket
Change the DAG's start_date to an earlier date

explanation: Tasks stuck in queued despite no code errors typically indicate the Celery worker fleet lacks capacity; increasing the environment size or maximum worker count relieves this bottleneck. Changing schedule_interval or start_date only affects when DAG runs are scheduled, and S3 bucket versioning has no effect on task execution capacity.

stem: A developer wants a Lambda function written in Python to programmatically start an existing AWS Glue ETL job whenever a new file lands in an S3 bucket. Which approach should the developer use inside the Lambda function code?

choices.text: Use the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) to call glue.start_job_run()
Use the AWS CLI installed on the Lambda execution environment to run aws glue start-job-run
Embed the Glue job's PySpark script directly inside the Lambda function
Configure an Amazon SQS FIFO queue to start the Glue job automatically without any code

explanation: Boto3, the AWS SDK for Python, is the standard supported way to call AWS service APIs such as Glue's start_job_run programmatically from Lambda code. The CLI is not a reliable dependency inside the Lambda runtime, a Glue Spark job cannot simply be embedded and run inside Lambda, and SQS alone cannot invoke a Glue API without an integration such as Lambda or Step Functions.

stem: A pipeline needs to pull data every hour from a third-party REST API that returns results across multiple pages, using a nextToken field in the JSON response to indicate more pages exist. Which approach correctly handles this inside a Lambda-based ingestion function?

choices.text: Make a single API call and assume all data is returned in that one response
Loop the API calls, passing the returned nextToken value into each subsequent request until no nextToken is returned
Increase the Lambda function's timeout so the API stops paginating
Configure Amazon API Gateway to automatically merge the third-party API's paginated responses

explanation: Correctly consuming a paginated API requires looping with the pagination token from each response until the API signals no further pages remain. Assuming a single response silently drops data, increasing the Lambda timeout does not change the API's pagination behavior, and API Gateway cannot automatically merge an external, third-party API's paginated payloads.

stem: Before running a full transformation pipeline, a data engineer wants to interactively explore a raw dataset, visually identify inconsistent formatting, and apply cleaning steps such as trimming whitespace and standardizing date formats, without writing custom Spark or Python code. Which service is designed for this?

choices.text: AWS Glue DataBrew
AWS Glue crawlers
Amazon Athena
AWS Step Functions

explanation: Glue DataBrew provides a visual, no-code interface with a large library of built-in transformations for interactively exploring and cleaning data. Crawlers only infer schema for the Data Catalog, Athena is a SQL query engine rather than a visual data-prep tool, and Step Functions is an orchestrator, not a cleaning tool.

stem: Which statement correctly describes Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio in the context of preparing data for analytics and ML workflows?

choices.text: It is a single web-based interface that brings together data preparation, SQL analytics, and ML/AI development tools in one collaborative workspace
It is a managed Apache Airflow environment for orchestrating ETL pipelines
It is a fully managed data warehouse optimized purely for OLAP queries
It is a service used exclusively for training and deploying deep learning models
It is a log analytics tool for searching and visualizing streaming application logs

explanation: SageMaker Unified Studio unifies data preparation, SQL-based analytics, and ML/AI development into one interface so teams can collaborate across the data-to-ML lifecycle. It is not an Airflow-based orchestrator, a data warehouse, a model-training-only service, or a log analytics tool.

stem: A data engineer wants to create a new, permanent table in the AWS Glue Data Catalog whose data is the materialized result of a complex Athena SQL query, stored as compressed Parquet files in S3, so downstream jobs can query it efficiently. Which Athena capability should be used?

choices.text: CREATE TABLE AS SELECT (CTAS)
A saved query
A named query with parameters
UNLOAD

explanation: CTAS materializes the results of a SELECT statement into new files (in a chosen format like Parquet) in S3 and registers the result as a new table in the Data Catalog. A saved or named query only stores the SQL text for reuse without materializing output, and UNLOAD writes query results to S3 but does not register a new Data Catalog table.

stem: A team wants a validation Lambda function to run automatically the moment a new object is uploaded to a specific S3 prefix, with no polling required. Which configuration achieves this?

choices.text: Configure an S3 event notification (or an EventBridge rule for S3 events) that invokes the Lambda function on s3:ObjectCreated events
Schedule an EventBridge rule that invokes the Lambda function every minute to check for new objects
Run the Lambda function inside a VPC and have it continuously poll the S3 bucket
Use AWS Config rules to detect new S3 objects and invoke Lambda

explanation: S3 event notifications (or S3 events routed through EventBridge) natively invoke a Lambda function immediately upon object creation, with no polling required. A minute-based cron rule adds latency and wasted invocations, VPC placement has nothing to do with detecting new objects, and AWS Config tracks resource configuration compliance rather than individual S3 object events.

stem: A company wants a Step Functions state machine to start automatically whenever an object matching a specific pattern is created in an S3 bucket, without writing custom polling code. Which combination of services achieves this?

choices.text: Enable EventBridge notifications from the S3 bucket, then create an EventBridge rule matching the object-created event pattern with the Step Functions state machine as the target
Configure the state machine to poll the S3 bucket every 5 minutes using a Wait state
Use AWS Config to detect the change and manually start the execution
Create an SNS topic with only an email subscription and manually start the execution when the email arrives

explanation: S3 can deliver events to EventBridge, and an EventBridge rule can match the object-created event pattern and directly target a Step Functions state machine, fully automating the trigger with no polling. Polling with Wait states wastes execution time and cost, AWS Config is meant for compliance tracking rather than event routing, and an email-only SNS subscription still requires a person to manually start the execution.

stem: A business analyst needs to build interactive, shareable dashboards with drill-downs for executives, while a data engineer separately needs to visually profile and clean a raw dataset before it is loaded for that dashboard. Which pairing of services correctly matches each need?

choices.text: Amazon QuickSight for the executive dashboards; AWS Glue DataBrew for profiling and cleaning the raw data
AWS Glue DataBrew for the executive dashboards; Amazon QuickSight for profiling and cleaning the raw data
Amazon Athena for the executive dashboards; Amazon EMR for profiling and cleaning
AWS Step Functions for the executive dashboards; AWS Lambda for profiling and cleaning

explanation: QuickSight is AWS's BI service built for interactive, shareable visualizations for business users, while DataBrew is purpose-built for visual data profiling and cleaning. The reversed pairing misapplies each tool, and the other options substitute a query engine or orchestration/compute services for dedicated visualization and cleaning tools.

stem: A data scientist wants to visually explore feature distributions, detect target leakage, and generate a bias report for a dataset intended for ML model training, all within a low-code visual interface, then export the resulting transforms as a reusable pipeline step. Which service is designed specifically for this?

choices.text: Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler
AWS Glue DataBrew
Amazon QuickSight
Amazon Athena

explanation: SageMaker Data Wrangler is built specifically for ML data preparation, including visual analyses such as bias detection and target leakage detection, with export to a reusable pipeline step. DataBrew focuses on general-purpose cleaning and profiling rather than ML-specific bias/leakage analyses, and QuickSight and Athena are visualization and query tools, not ML data-prep tools.

stem: A data engineer wants to interactively run Python code, view intermediate DataFrame outputs, and document analysis steps with narrative text while verifying a newly ingested dataset. Which tool is best suited to this exploratory, code-first verification workflow?

choices.text: A Jupyter notebook, such as one hosted through Amazon SageMaker Studio
An AWS Glue crawler
An Amazon CloudWatch dashboard
AWS Config

explanation: Jupyter notebooks provide an interactive, cell-based environment combining code, output, and narrative markdown, well suited to exploratory data verification. Glue crawlers only populate the Data Catalog with schema metadata, CloudWatch dashboards visualize operational metrics rather than arbitrary code-driven exploration, and AWS Config tracks resource configuration rather than dataset content.

stem: An analyst runs the following Athena query: SELECT region, SUM(amount) AS total_sales FROM sales GROUP BY region HAVING SUM(amount) > 100000; What does this query return?

choices.text: Each region's total sales, but only for regions whose total sales exceed 100000
Every individual sales row where the amount column exceeds 100000
Only the single region with the highest total sales
An error, because HAVING cannot be used together with an aggregate function like SUM

explanation: GROUP BY aggregates rows per region and HAVING filters on the aggregated SUM result, so only regions whose total exceeds 100000 appear in the output. HAVING is designed to filter on aggregates (unlike WHERE), option B describes row-level filtering instead of aggregation, and option C would require an ORDER BY with LIMIT 1, which is not present.

stem: In Amazon Redshift, which SQL construct correctly computes, for each row, a 7-day rolling average of daily_sales ordered by sale_date?

choices.text: AVG(daily_sales) OVER (ORDER BY sale_date ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
AVG(daily_sales) GROUP BY sale_date
SUM(daily_sales) / COUNT(*) with no OVER or GROUP BY clause
AVG(daily_sales) OVER (PARTITION BY sale_date)

explanation: A window function with ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, ordered by date, averages the current row and the prior 6 rows for each row, producing a 7-day rolling average. GROUP BY collapses rows into one result per date rather than a per-row rolling value, a plain aggregate without OVER/GROUP BY returns a single table-wide value, and PARTITION BY sale_date would isolate every date into its own single-row partition instead of a rolling window.

stem: What capability does running an Athena notebook on Apache Spark provide that standard Athena SQL queries do not?

choices.text: The ability to run interactive PySpark code, including custom transformations and Spark libraries, against data in S3 within the same Athena workgroup
The ability to store query results permanently without using Amazon S3
The ability to bypass the AWS Glue Data Catalog entirely for all table metadata
Automatic creation of Amazon QuickSight dashboards from query results

explanation: Athena's Spark support enables interactive, notebook-based PySpark sessions that run custom transformations and use Spark libraries, going beyond SQL-only querying. Athena still relies on S3 for result and data storage, still typically integrates with the Glue Data Catalog for metadata, and does not automatically generate QuickSight dashboards.

stem: A startup's Redshift analytics workload is highly unpredictable: some weeks see almost no queries, while a monthly reporting cycle produces a two-day spike of heavy queries. The team wants to minimize cost during idle periods while still handling the spike, without manually resizing clusters. Which approach best fits this pattern?

choices.text: Amazon Redshift Serverless, which automatically scales compute capacity based on workload and charges based on usage
A single fixed-size provisioned Redshift cluster sized for the monthly peak, running continuously
A provisioned Redshift cluster paused every night regardless of actual workload
An Amazon EMR cluster running Presto configured to replace Redshift

explanation: Redshift Serverless automatically scales measured capacity up during the spike and down during idle periods, aligning cost with actual usage for unpredictable workloads. A fixed cluster sized for peak wastes money while idle, nightly pausing does not address unpredictable intraday or weekly spikes, and replacing Redshift with Presto on EMR is not a reasonable or equivalent substitute.

stem: A dataset has one row per (product, month, sales_amount). An analyst wants to reshape it so each row represents one product, with a separate column for each month's sales_amount. Which operation accomplishes this transformation?

choices.text: A pivot operation
A UNION ALL of the rows
An INNER JOIN of the table with itself
A GROUP BY clause with no aggregate function

explanation: A pivot operation turns the unique values of one column (month) into separate new columns, converting long-format data into wide-format, which is exactly the transformation needed here. UNION ALL only stacks rows, a self-join would combine or duplicate rows rather than reshape columns, and GROUP BY without an aggregate function is not a valid way to pivot data.

stem: A pipeline needs a lightweight, event-driven check that runs immediately after each file lands in S3 to verify basic structure (for example, confirming a header row exists and required columns are present) before downstream processing continues. Which approach is most appropriate?

choices.text: An S3 event triggers a Lambda function that performs the lightweight validation logic and signals success or failure to the pipeline
A permanently running EMR cluster polls S3 every second to validate incoming files
A QuickSight dashboard is manually reviewed each morning for anomalies
An Athena CREATE TABLE statement is used to validate file structure once a week

explanation: An S3 event notification triggering a Lambda function provides fast, event-driven, lightweight validation immediately upon file arrival, matching this scenario well. A permanently running EMR cluster for this purpose is costly and unnecessary, manual dashboard review is not automated or immediate, and a weekly check would leave issues undetected for days.

stem: Which AWS service records a history of API calls made within an AWS account, including who made the call, when, and from which source IP, and is commonly used to support security and operational auditing?

choices.text: AWS CloudTrail
Amazon CloudWatch Logs
AWS Config
Amazon Macie

explanation: CloudTrail records API activity across AWS services, capturing who called what, when, and from where, for governance and audit purposes. CloudWatch Logs stores application or service log data rather than a dedicated API call history, AWS Config tracks resource configuration state and changes rather than API calls, and Macie discovers and classifies sensitive data rather than logging API activity.

stem: By default, where can a data engineer view the driver and executor logs generated by an AWS Glue Spark ETL job run?

choices.text: Amazon CloudWatch Logs, under log groups associated with the Glue job
AWS CloudTrail event history
Amazon S3 Glacier
The AWS Config resource timeline

explanation: Glue job runs automatically send output and error logs to CloudWatch Logs, organized into log groups and streams viewable from the Glue console or CloudWatch. CloudTrail records API calls like StartJobRun rather than job execution output, S3 Glacier is archival storage Glue does not write logs to directly, and AWS Config tracks resource configuration rather than job logs.

stem: A team wants to be notified by email within minutes whenever an AWS Glue job fails. Which combination of services accomplishes this?

choices.text: An EventBridge rule (or CloudWatch alarm) on the Glue job's failure state, publishing to an SNS topic with an email subscription
An AWS Config rule that emails the team once a day with a compliance summary
A manually run Athena query on Glue job history each morning
A CloudTrail Insights report scheduled to run weekly

explanation: An EventBridge rule that detects the Glue job's FAILED state can publish to an SNS topic, and an email subscription on that topic delivers near-real-time notification. Daily Config summaries and weekly CloudTrail Insights reports operate on a much slower cadence, and a manual morning check introduces unacceptable delay for timely alerting.

stem: An AWS Glue Spark job repeatedly fails with out-of-memory errors on the executors when processing a large dataset, though the same job succeeds on smaller datasets. Which change is most likely to resolve this?

choices.text: Increase the number of workers or the worker type (DPU allocation) for the Glue job
Change the job's IAM role to use AdministratorAccess
Decrease the job's timeout parameter
Switch the job type from PySpark to a Python shell job

explanation: Out-of-memory errors that appear only at larger data volumes typically indicate insufficient compute resources; increasing worker count or moving to a larger worker type gives each executor more memory and parallelism. IAM permissions do not affect available memory, decreasing the timeout only makes the job fail sooner, and Python shell jobs run single-node and are not intended for large-scale distributed Spark processing.

stem: An EMR cluster using EC2 Spot Instances for task nodes experiences intermittent job failures correlated with Spot Instance interruption notices, while the master and core nodes run On-Demand. What is the best practice to reduce failures caused by these interruptions?

choices.text: Keep Spot Instances limited to task nodes (which hold no HDFS data), and use EMR instance fleets with multiple instance types to improve Spot availability and resilience
Move the master node to Spot Instances as well, to save additional cost
Store all HDFS data exclusively on the Spot task nodes for faster local access
Disable YARN node health checks so interrupted nodes are not removed from the cluster

explanation: Task nodes are the correct place for Spot capacity because they hold no HDFS data, and diversifying instance types via instance fleets improves the chance of obtaining and retaining Spot capacity. Moving the master node to Spot risks losing control of the entire cluster on interruption, storing HDFS data on Spot task nodes risks data loss, and disabling health checks would let the cluster keep scheduling work on instances about to disappear, worsening failures.

stem: A data engineer wants to find the count of ERROR-level log entries per 5-minute interval across a Lambda function's CloudWatch log group over the last 24 hours, without exporting the logs anywhere else. Which tool should be used?

choices.text: CloudWatch Logs Insights, using a query such as stats count() by bin(5m) filtered on the ERROR pattern
Amazon Athena, after manually copying the logs into S3 first
The AWS X-Ray service map
AWS Trusted Advisor

explanation: CloudWatch Logs Insights provides a purpose-built query language that runs directly against CloudWatch Logs, supporting pattern filtering and time-bucketed aggregation with bin(), with no data movement required. Athena would require exporting the logs to S3 first, X-Ray shows distributed tracing and service maps rather than log-level error counts, and Trusted Advisor provides account best-practice checks, not log analysis.

stem: A team has VPC Flow Logs and ALB access logs delivered to an S3 bucket in a consistent partitioned format. They want to run complex, ad hoc SQL joins across both log types to investigate a security incident, without provisioning any servers. Which service is best suited?

choices.text: Amazon Athena, querying both log sets directly from S3 using SQL
AWS CloudTrail Insights
Amazon Inspector
AWS Trusted Advisor

explanation: Athena is a serverless, SQL-based query engine built to run ad hoc, complex queries, including joins, directly against log data in S3, with no servers to provision. CloudTrail Insights only detects unusual API activity patterns, Amazon Inspector performs vulnerability scanning, and Trusted Advisor gives account configuration recommendations, none of which support ad hoc SQL joins across arbitrary log files.

stem: A team wants to build a near-real-time, interactive dashboard for searching and visualizing streaming application logs, including full-text search across log messages. Which AWS service is purpose-built for this use case?

choices.text: Amazon OpenSearch Service
Amazon Redshift
The AWS Glue Data Catalog
Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive

explanation: OpenSearch Service is designed for full-text search and log analytics, with near-real-time interactive dashboards through OpenSearch Dashboards, making it well suited for searching streaming logs. Redshift is a SQL data warehouse rather than a full-text search engine, the Glue Data Catalog only stores table metadata, and S3 Glacier Deep Archive is cold storage unsuitable for near-real-time interactive search.

stem: Users report that ad hoc analytical queries in Amazon Redshift are taking much longer than usual to start executing, even though the queries themselves are simple. Reviewing the cluster shows many queries queued concurrently. Which action is most likely to address this?

choices.text: Review and adjust Workload Management (WLM) queue configuration, such as increasing concurrency or adding a separate queue for ad hoc queries
Enable S3 bucket versioning on the underlying data lake
Add read replicas to the Redshift cluster
Convert all analytical queries into stored procedures

explanation: Long wait times before execution begins typically indicate a Workload Management concurrency bottleneck, so adjusting WLM queues (separate queues, increased concurrency, or automatic WLM) directly addresses the queuing delay. Redshift does not support RDS-style read replicas, S3 versioning is unrelated to query queuing, and converting queries into stored procedures does not resolve concurrency contention.

stem: A team wants to track, over time, the number of AWS Glue job runs that succeed versus fail. Which native AWS Glue integration provides this metric data without any custom instrumentation?

choices.text: Amazon CloudWatch metrics automatically published by AWS Glue for job run status
AWS Trusted Advisor cost checks
Amazon Macie sensitive data findings
AWS License Manager usage reports

explanation: AWS Glue automatically emits CloudWatch metrics, including job run success and failure counts, with no custom instrumentation needed, and these can be graphed or alarmed on. Trusted Advisor focuses on cost, security, and performance best-practice checks, Macie is for sensitive data discovery, and License Manager tracks software license usage, none of which report Glue job run status.

stem: A data engineer wants an AWS Glue ETL job's data quality check to automatically fail if more than 2% of rows have a null value in the customer_id column. Which approach should be used?

choices.text: Define an AWS Glue Data Quality ruleset using DQDL with a completeness/null-percentage rule on customer_id, and configure the job to fail on rule violation
Manually inspect a sample of rows in the Athena console after each job run
Add a CHECK constraint on the destination Redshift table
Rely on the Glue crawler to detect and automatically reject rows with a null customer_id

explanation: AWS Glue Data Quality lets you define rules in DQDL, including checks on the completeness or null percentage of a column, and configure the job to fail or alert when rules are violated. Manual sampling does not scale or run automatically, a Redshift CHECK constraint would not apply during the Glue ETL stage, and crawlers only infer schema, they do not reject or validate row-level data quality.

stem: A data engineer suspects that a column expected to contain only US state abbreviations actually contains inconsistent values, such as full state names mixed with abbreviations and some typos. Which DataBrew feature would most directly help investigate this before deciding on cleaning rules?

choices.text: Run a DataBrew data profile job on the dataset and review the column's value distribution and unique value counts
Immediately delete the column from the dataset
Export the dataset unmodified to Amazon Redshift
Increase the DataBrew project's sample size setting without reviewing any output

explanation: A DataBrew profile job computes column-level statistics, including value distributions and unique values, which surfaces exactly this kind of inconsistency before defining cleaning transforms. Deleting the column discards potentially valuable data without investigation, exporting unmodified data elsewhere does not address the quality issue, and increasing sample size without reviewing output provides no insight.

stem: A data engineer wants to profile a 500 GB dataset in AWS Glue DataBrew but needs the sample to proportionally represent each category in a highly imbalanced customer_segment column, rather than just taking the first N rows. Which sampling approach is most appropriate?

choices.text: Stratified sampling, which selects rows to preserve the relative proportions of each category
Sequential sampling, taking only the first 500 rows in the file's original order
Sampling only the most recent 24 hours of data regardless of category distribution
Using the entire 500 GB dataset with no sampling on every profiling run

explanation: Stratified sampling deliberately selects records so each subgroup, such as each customer_segment category, is proportionally represented, which matters for imbalanced categorical data. Sequential or first-N sampling can badly misrepresent an imbalanced distribution, recency-based filtering ignores the category-representation goal, and using the full dataset defeats the time and cost benefit of sampling.

stem: In the context of distributed data processing, such as Apache Spark running on Amazon EMR or AWS Glue, what does data skew refer to?

choices.text: An uneven distribution of data across partitions, causing some tasks or nodes to process significantly more data than others and become a processing bottleneck
A discrepancy between a dataset's declared schema and its actual data types
The gradual decline of a machine learning model's accuracy over time
A misconfigured IAM policy that grants a Glue job excessive permissions

explanation: Data skew occurs when data is unevenly distributed across partitions or keys, so some tasks or executors handle disproportionately more data and become bottlenecks while others sit idle. Schema-type mismatches, model accuracy drift, and IAM misconfiguration are distinct concepts with different causes and symptoms.

stem: A Spark job on EMR performs a groupByKey/join on a customer_id field, but a small number of power-user customer_id values account for a disproportionate share of all records, causing a few tasks to run far longer than the rest and stall the entire job. Which technique is most effective at mitigating this data skew?

choices.text: Apply salting: add a random suffix to the skewed key to spread its records across multiple partitions before the join/aggregation, then combine the partial results
Reduce the number of Spark executors to force more sequential processing
Repartition the data into a single partition to guarantee even distribution
Disable Spark's speculative execution entirely

explanation: Salting artificially splits a heavily skewed key into several sub-keys distributed across partitions, balancing the workload before combining results, a standard technique for mitigating key skew in joins and aggregations. Reducing executors or collapsing to a single partition would make the imbalance and bottleneck worse, and disabling speculative execution addresses straggler tasks from unrelated causes, not the root skew.

stem: A team configures a DataBrew data quality rule checking that the email column matches a valid email pattern, with a threshold requiring at least 95% of rows to pass. If a run shows 92% of rows matching the pattern, what is the outcome?

choices.text: The rule fails, because the passing percentage (92%) is below the configured 95% threshold
The rule automatically passes, because DataBrew rounds thresholds up to the nearest whole dataset
The ruleset is skipped entirely because the threshold was not met exactly
DataBrew halts all data quality monitoring for the entire AWS account until manually reset

explanation: A DataBrew data quality rule with a percentage threshold fails whenever the actual passing percentage falls below the configured minimum, so 92% against a 95% requirement results in a failed rule. DataBrew does not round thresholds to force a pass, it evaluates rather than skips a rule when the threshold is not met, and a single failed rule does not halt account-wide monitoring.

stem: A data engineer is building an AWS Lambda function that reads objects from an Amazon S3 bucket and writes processed results to another S3 bucket. The company requires that credentials never be hardcoded and that the function only has the minimum permissions needed. Which approach should the engineer use to grant the Lambda function access to the S3 buckets?

choices.text: Create an IAM user with an access key and secret key, and store the credentials as Lambda environment variables
Attach an IAM execution role to the Lambda function with a policy that grants only the required S3 actions on the specific buckets
Embed the AWS account root credentials in the function code
Configure a VPC security group rule that allows the Lambda function to reach S3

explanation: Lambda functions should use an IAM execution role, to which AWS automatically supplies temporary credentials, eliminating the need for long-lived access keys. Option A stores static credentials which violates security best practice, and security groups (D) control network traffic, not permissions to AWS APIs.

stem: Which AWS Secrets Manager capability allows a database password to be automatically changed on a schedule without requiring application downtime, using a Lambda function that AWS provides or that you customize?

choices.text: Secrets Manager resource policies
Secrets Manager automatic rotation
Parameter Store advanced parameters
IAM credential reports

explanation: Secrets Manager automatic rotation uses a rotation Lambda function to update the credential in both the secret and the target database on a defined schedule. Resource policies (A) control who can access the secret rather than rotating it, and Parameter Store advanced parameters (C) do not provide built-in database credential rotation.

stem: An Amazon EC2-hosted ETL job needs to write data to an Amazon S3 bucket but must never traverse the public internet. The security team also requires that the traffic be controlled through a resource-level endpoint policy in addition to IAM permissions. Which change should the data engineer make?

choices.text: Add an inbound rule to the EC2 security group allowing traffic to S3's public IP range
Create a Gateway VPC endpoint for S3 and attach an endpoint policy restricting access to the required bucket
Attach an internet gateway to the private subnet
Create a NAT gateway and route S3 traffic through it

explanation: A Gateway VPC endpoint for S3 keeps traffic on the AWS network and supports an endpoint policy that further restricts which S3 resources can be reached, satisfying both requirements. Security group rules (A) cannot control routing to public IPs for this purpose, and a NAT gateway (D) would still send traffic to the public S3 endpoint over an internet-routed path.

stem: A team is exposing a data ingestion pipeline through Amazon API Gateway, which must invoke a backend AWS Lambda function. What is the correct way to grant API Gateway permission to invoke the Lambda function?

choices.text: Create an IAM user for API Gateway and store its access keys in the Lambda function
Grant API Gateway a resource-based permission on the Lambda function (or use an invocation role) that allows the lambda:InvokeFunction action
Make the Lambda function public by removing all resource policies
Configure a VPC peering connection between API Gateway and Lambda

explanation: API Gateway needs either a Lambda resource-based policy granting it invoke permission, or an IAM role it assumes with lambda:InvokeFunction permission; this is the standard, least-privilege integration pattern. Storing IAM user keys (A) is unnecessary and insecure, and VPC peering (D) is unrelated since API Gateway invokes Lambda through the Lambda API, not a VPC connection.

stem: In the AWS shared responsibility model, which statement correctly distinguishes a managed service like Amazon RDS from an unmanaged (self-managed) deployment such as a database running on Amazon EC2, with respect to authentication infrastructure?

choices.text: AWS manages patching of the underlying database engine and host OS for RDS, but the customer must patch the OS and manage host-level authentication for a database self-hosted on EC2
AWS manages patching for both RDS and self-hosted EC2 databases equally
The customer must patch the underlying host OS for RDS in addition to managing IAM
IAM authentication is unavailable for both RDS and EC2-hosted databases

explanation: For a managed service like RDS, AWS handles OS and engine patching and offers IAM database authentication as an option, whereas a self-managed database on EC2 requires the customer to patch the OS and manage local authentication mechanisms. Options B and C misstate the split of responsibilities, and D is incorrect since RDS supports IAM database authentication.

stem: A central platform team wants to deploy a standard set of IAM roles and logging resources across 40 AWS member accounts in an organization using AWS CloudFormation StackSets, without manually assuming a role in each account. What must be configured first?

choices.text: An AWS Config aggregator in the management account
Trusted access for CloudFormation StackSets enabled in AWS Organizations, plus service-managed permissions
A Secrets Manager secret replicated to every member account
An S3 bucket policy granting PutObject to every account ID

explanation: Deploying StackSets across an organization requires enabling trusted access for CloudFormation StackSets in AWS Organizations and using service-managed permissions, which automatically creates the necessary IAM roles in member accounts. An AWS Config aggregator (A) is for compliance visibility, not deployment permissions, and neither a Secrets Manager secret nor an S3 bucket policy (C, D) provides the cross-account execution role StackSets requires.

stem: Within Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, which hierarchy correctly describes how access and resources are organized for teams collaborating on data and ML assets?

choices.text: A single global namespace shared by all AWS accounts with no further subdivision
A domain contains domain units, and domain units contain projects that scope membership and resource access for a team's work
Projects contain domains, and domains contain IAM users directly
Access is controlled solely through S3 bucket policies with no domain concept

explanation: SageMaker Unified Studio organizes collaboration through a domain, which can be subdivided into domain units, under which projects are created to scope members, data, and compute resources for a given initiative. The other options invert or omit this hierarchy and do not reflect how Unified Studio structures access.

stem: A data engineer must grant a group of analysts permission to run Amazon Athena queries only against tables in a specific Glue Data Catalog database, and must not allow them to modify or delete tables. Which approach best follows least privilege?

choices.text: Attach the AdministratorAccess managed policy to the analysts' IAM group
Create a custom IAM policy that allows only the required read-only Glue and Athena actions, scoped to the specific database ARN, and attach it to the analysts' group
Grant the analysts IAM users root account access
Use the AmazonAthenaFullAccess managed policy for all analysts

explanation: A custom policy scoped to only the read actions and the specific database ARN grants exactly the permissions needed and nothing more, satisfying least privilege. AdministratorAccess and AmazonAthenaFullAccess (A, D) grant far broader permissions than required, including the ability to modify or delete resources.

stem: A company needs to store a database password that an application retrieves at runtime, and separately needs to store a non-sensitive application configuration value like a table name. Which combination is most appropriate and cost-effective?

choices.text: Store both values in AWS Secrets Manager
Store the database password in AWS Secrets Manager and the configuration value in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store as a standard parameter
Store both values in Systems Manager Parameter Store as SecureString parameters
Store both values as Lambda environment variables in plaintext

explanation: Secrets Manager is purpose-built for secrets like database credentials, offering automatic rotation, while Parameter Store standard parameters are a free, simple option for non-sensitive configuration values, making this combination most cost-effective. Storing everything in Secrets Manager (A) incurs unnecessary cost for non-sensitive data, and plaintext environment variables (D) expose the password insecurely.

stem: A company wants IAM permissions to automatically apply to any new Amazon S3 bucket that is tagged with project=analytics, without editing the policy each time a new bucket is created. Which authorization approach does this describe?

choices.text: Role-based access control using a fixed list of bucket ARNs
Attribute-based access control (ABAC) using resource tags as a condition in the IAM policy
Network-based access control using security groups
Discretionary access control using S3 bucket ACLs

explanation: ABAC uses tags as attributes in IAM policy conditions, so a single policy automatically applies to any resource carrying the matching tag, including future ones, without policy edits. Role-based access with a fixed ARN list (A) would require updating the policy each time a new bucket is created, and security groups (C) do not control S3 API authorization.

stem: A rapidly growing organization is deciding between a purely role-based access control (RBAC) model, where a new IAM role is created for every job function and resource combination, and an attribute-based access control (ABAC) model using tags for the same access requirements. What is a key operational tradeoff of choosing RBAC over ABAC as the number of teams and resources scales?

choices.text: RBAC requires no policy management at all once created

RBAC can lead to significant role and policy sprawl, requiring new roles and policy updates for each new resource or team, whereas ABAC scales more easily by tagging resources and principals consistently
ABAC cannot be implemented in IAM at all
RBAC automatically inherits permissions from resource tags without configuration

explanation: As organizations scale, RBAC often requires creating and maintaining many discrete roles and policies for each new combination of resource and job function, causing sprawl, while ABAC lets a smaller set of policies use tag conditions to scale automatically. Option A is false since RBAC still requires ongoing policy maintenance, and C is incorrect because IAM natively supports ABAC through tag-based conditions.

stem: A database administrator needs to give a new analyst read-only access to specific tables in an Amazon Redshift database, following the principle of granting access through database-level roles rather than the AWS account's IAM policies. Which SQL approach should be used?

choices.text: Modify the cluster's IAM role attached at the Redshift cluster level
Create a database user, add the user to a group with SELECT privileges via GRANT statements, or assign a Redshift role with the needed privileges
Update the VPC security group inbound rules for the analyst's IP address
Create an AWS Secrets Manager rotation schedule for the analyst

explanation: Redshift supports native database users, groups, and roles managed with SQL GRANT statements, allowing fine-grained, database-level authorization independent of the cluster's IAM role. The cluster IAM role (A) governs the cluster's access to other AWS services, not individual user privileges within the database, and security groups (C) only control network-level connectivity.

stem: An IAM role has an attached policy that allows glue:GetTable and s3:GetObject on a Lake Formation-governed table, but when the role's user tries to query the table through Amazon Athena, the query fails with an access denied error. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The IAM policy syntax is invalid JSON
The role has IAM permissions but has not also been granted the corresponding Lake Formation permissions (such as SELECT) on the table
Athena does not support Lake Formation-governed tables
The S3 bucket has been deleted

explanation: For Lake Formation-governed resources, both IAM permissions and separate Lake Formation permissions (grants such as SELECT on the table) must be in place; without the Lake Formation grant, access is denied even if IAM allows it. Athena fully supports Lake Formation-governed tables, and if the bucket were deleted the crawler and catalog would show broader errors rather than just an access-denied result on an otherwise valid query.

stem: A team is configuring encryption for a new Amazon S3 bucket using AWS KMS (SSE-KMS). They must decide who can use the KMS key to decrypt objects. Which statement correctly distinguishes the roles of the KMS key policy and an IAM policy attached to a user in this scenario?

choices.text: The IAM policy alone is sufficient; the KMS key policy is ignored for cross-service encryption
Both the KMS key policy must allow the principal to use the key (directly or via a delegated IAM policy) and the caller's IAM policy must allow the KMS actions; access is denied if either is missing
Only the KMS key policy matters; IAM policies have no effect on KMS key usage
S3 bucket policies alone control KMS key usage

explanation: KMS keys evaluate both the key's resource policy and the caller's IAM policy (unless the key policy explicitly delegates all authorization to IAM); both must permit the action for access to succeed. Options A and C each ignore one of the two required layers of authorization, and S3 bucket policies (D) control S3 object access but do not by themselves authorize KMS key usage.

stem: A company wants to ensure that all requests to its Amazon S3 bucket, whether from applications or users, are rejected unless they use HTTPS, to guarantee encryption in transit. Which solution enforces this requirement?

choices.text: Enable default SSE-S3 encryption on the bucket
Add a bucket policy statement that denies requests where aws:SecureTransport is false
Enable S3 Versioning on the bucket
Attach a VPC endpoint policy only, with no bucket policy change

explanation: A bucket policy with a Deny statement conditioned on aws:SecureTransport being false blocks any non-HTTPS request, directly enforcing encryption in transit. Default encryption (A) protects data at rest but does not affect the transport protocol, and Versioning (C) is unrelated to transit encryption.

stem: A healthcare analytics team needs to let data scientists query a Redshift table containing patient names and SSNs, but must automatically show only partially obscured values (such as the last four digits of an SSN) to users without elevated privileges, while showing full values to privileged users. Which capability addresses this requirement?

choices.text: Redshift dynamic data masking
Cross-region snapshot copy
Redshift Spectrum
Enhanced VPC routing

explanation: Redshift dynamic data masking applies masking policies at query time so that different users see full or obscured values for sensitive columns based on their granted privileges, without duplicating data. Redshift Spectrum (C) is for querying data in S3 and enhanced VPC routing (D) affects network paths, neither of which masks column values.

stem: Account A owns an Amazon S3 bucket with objects encrypted using a customer managed AWS KMS key. Account B needs to read those objects using a role in its own account. What must be configured to allow this cross-account decryption?

choices.text: Nothing; KMS keys work across accounts by default

The KMS key policy in Account A must grant Account B's role permission to use the key (kms:Decrypt), and an IAM policy in Account B must also allow the role to call KMS actions, in addition to S3 permissions on the bucket/objects
Account B must create its own copy of the KMS key
Only the S3 bucket policy needs to be updated; KMS permissions are not required across accounts

explanation: Cross-account use of a customer managed KMS key requires the key policy to explicitly grant the external account or principal permission, and the calling account must also authorize its principal via IAM policy; S3 permissions alone are insufficient when SSE-KMS is used. KMS access is not automatic across accounts (ruling out A), and an account cannot create its own copy of another account's key material (C).

stem: Which encryption approach means that data is encrypted by the client application before it is ever sent over the network to AWS, so that AWS never has access to the plaintext data or the encryption key?

choices.text: Server-side encryption with Amazon S3-managed keys (SSE-S3)
Client-side encryption
Server-side encryption with AWS KMS-managed keys (SSE-KMS)
In-transit TLS encryption only

explanation: Client-side encryption encrypts data locally, before transmission, using keys the client manages, so AWS services store and transmit only ciphertext. SSE-S3 and SSE-KMS (A, C) both encrypt data on the server side after it arrives at AWS, and TLS alone (D) protects data in transit but the object itself may still be stored in plaintext without additional server-side encryption.

stem: An application that has been successfully decrypting data for months suddenly cannot decrypt newly retrieved older ciphertext, after the customer manually created a new AWS KMS customer managed key and re-pointed an existing alias to it. What most likely explains the behavior?

choices.text: KMS deleted the old key material immediately, which is expected behavior for all rotations

Re-pointing an alias to a new CMK means data newly encrypted uses the new underlying key, but data previously encrypted with the old CMK must still be decrypted using that original CMK, which must still exist and be enabled
KMS automatically re-encrypts all previously encrypted objects when an alias is updated
This indicates a Secrets Manager rotation failure, unrelated to KMS

explanation: When an alias is manually re-pointed to a new customer managed key, old ciphertext remains tied to the original CMK's key ID embedded in the ciphertext metadata, so that original key must remain enabled to decrypt older data. KMS does not automatically re-encrypt existing ciphertext when an alias changes (ruling out C), and this scenario is unrelated to Secrets Manager (D).

stem: A company must both discover unclassified sensitive data such as PII scattered across S3 buckets and also mask sensitive columns before analysts query a Redshift table. Which pairing of services correctly addresses each need respectively?

choices.text: Amazon Macie for discovering PII in S3, and Redshift dynamic data masking for masking query results
AWS Config for discovering PII, and AWS KMS for masking query results
Amazon GuardDuty for discovering PII, and Amazon Macie for masking query results
AWS CloudTrail for discovering PII, and IAM policies for masking query results

explanation: Amazon Macie uses machine learning and pattern matching to discover and classify sensitive data like PII in S3, while Redshift's dynamic data masking capability obscures sensitive column values for less-privileged users at query time. AWS Config (B) tracks configuration compliance rather than scanning data content, and GuardDuty (C) is a threat detection service, not a data classification tool.

stem: A global company operates workloads in two AWS Regions and needs both regions to be able to decrypt the same encrypted data using AWS KMS, with the ability to fail over encryption operations to the second Region during a Regional disruption, while keeping a single logical key identity. Which KMS feature should be used?

choices.text: A single-Region customer managed key shared through IAM cross-account policies
AWS KMS multi-Region keys, replicated as related keys in each Region with the same key material
AWS managed keys (aws/s3)
Enabling automatic annual key rotation

explanation: KMS multi-Region keys let you create replica keys in multiple Regions that share the same key material and key ID, so ciphertext encrypted in one Region can be decrypted in another without re-encrypting data, supporting disaster recovery scenarios. A single-Region key (A) cannot be used directly in another Region, and AWS managed keys (C) cannot be created as multi-Region keys under customer control.

stem: A security team wants to run SQL-based queries across CloudTrail events aggregated from multiple AWS accounts and Regions, retained for up to several years, without having to first load data into S3 and set up Athena tables manually. Which service best fits this requirement?

choices.text: Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights
AWS CloudTrail Lake
Amazon OpenSearch Service
AWS Config aggregator

explanation: CloudTrail Lake is a managed, immutable data store purpose-built for running SQL queries against CloudTrail events aggregated across accounts and Regions with configurable long-term retention, without manual Athena table setup. CloudWatch Logs Insights (A) queries log groups rather than natively aggregating CloudTrail events across accounts in this way, and an AWS Config aggregator (D) is for configuration compliance data, not CloudTrail events.

stem: An organization already delivers its CloudTrail logs to a centralized Amazon S3 bucket and wants to run ad hoc SQL queries against historical logs stored as JSON/gzip files without deploying additional infrastructure. Which service is the most direct fit?

choices.text: Amazon Athena with a table defined over the CloudTrail S3 log location
Amazon Redshift Spectrum with a mandatory ETL pipeline
AWS Glue DataBrew
Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics

explanation: Athena can directly query CloudTrail's JSON log files stored in S3 using a serverless, SQL-based approach with no infrastructure to manage, and AWS even provides a CloudTrail table creation helper. Redshift Spectrum (B) would work but implies a Redshift cluster and more setup than described, and Kinesis Data Analytics (D) is designed for streaming data, not static historical log files.

stem: A team must decide between using Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights and Amazon Athena to analyze several terabytes of historical application log data that is already archived in Amazon S3 in Parquet format for infrequent, ad hoc investigations. What is a key tradeoff to consider?

choices.text: CloudWatch Logs Insights natively queries data stored in S3 in Parquet format with no additional configuration, making it strictly better for this use case

CloudWatch Logs Insights is designed to query logs within CloudWatch Logs log groups and does not directly query S3-archived Parquet files, whereas Athena can query the S3 data directly and cost-effectively for infrequent queries without ingesting it into CloudWatch Logs
Athena cannot query Parquet files under any circumstances
Both services are functionally identical for this scenario with no meaningful differences

explanation: CloudWatch Logs Insights operates on log groups ingested into CloudWatch Logs, so S3-archived Parquet files would need to be reingested to use it, whereas Athena queries data directly in S3 and is well suited to infrequent, ad hoc analysis of already-archived Parquet data. Option A is factually incorrect, and Athena has strong native support for Parquet, contradicting option C.

stem: A security engineer configured an AWS CloudTrail trail expecting it to capture PutObject and DeleteObject events for a sensitive S3 bucket, but the trail's event history only shows CreateBucket and PutBucketPolicy events for that bucket. What most likely explains the gap?

choices.text: The trail is only configured to log management events, not data events, for that S3 bucket
CloudTrail cannot log any S3 events under any configuration
The S3 bucket has server-side encryption disabled
The IAM role used by the application lacks a trust policy

explanation: CreateBucket and PutBucketPolicy are management events, which are logged by default, while PutObject and DeleteObject are data events that must be explicitly enabled for the specific bucket (or all S3 buckets) in the trail configuration. CloudTrail fully supports logging S3 data events (ruling out B), and neither encryption settings nor a trust policy issue would selectively suppress only data events while management events still appear.

stem: A compliance team wants to be notified in near real time whenever a CloudTrail event shows that an IAM policy was attached granting administrator-level permissions to any user. Which integration should be built?

choices.text: Configure an Amazon EventBridge rule that matches the specific CloudTrail API call pattern and triggers an SNS notification or Lambda function
Manually review the CloudTrail console once a day
Enable S3 default encryption on the CloudTrail log bucket
Create an AWS Config conformance pack with no further action

explanation: CloudTrail events can be delivered to EventBridge in near real time, so a rule matching the specific IAM API call (such as AttachUserPolicy with an administrator policy ARN) can automatically trigger an SNS notification or a Lambda remediation function. Manual daily review (B) is not near real time, and enabling encryption (C) does not provide alerting.

stem: A company ingests application and infrastructure logs from many sources and wants a centralized platform to build interactive dashboards, run full-text search, and visualize log trends over time across a large fleet. Which service is best suited to this centralized log analytics and visualization use case?

choices.text: AWS Config
Amazon OpenSearch Service
AWS Secrets Manager
AWS Key Management Service

explanation: Amazon OpenSearch Service is designed for centralized log analytics, full-text search, and building interactive visual dashboards across large volumes of log data. AWS Config (A) tracks resource configuration compliance rather than general log analytics, and Secrets Manager and KMS (C, D) are unrelated to log visualization.

stem: What does Amazon Redshift data sharing allow a data provider cluster or workgroup to do?

choices.text: Copy entire databases to another account nightly using COPY commands only
Grant live, read access to specific databases, schemas, or tables to other Redshift clusters or workgroups, including in different AWS accounts, without copying or moving the underlying data
Automatically encrypt all shared data with a new KMS key for each consumer
Export data to Amazon S3 in Parquet format for external querying only

explanation: Redshift data sharing provides live, secure access to selected data objects across Redshift clusters or workgroups, including across accounts and Regions, without duplicating or moving the data, enabling low-latency collaboration. Option A describes a batch copy pattern, not data sharing, and option D describes unloading data to S3 rather than the direct cluster-to-cluster sharing that Redshift data sharing provides.

stem: A governance team wants to automatically discover columns containing PII across many S3-based data lake tables and then enforce that only authorized roles can query those specific columns through the data lake's catalog. Which combination of services and workflow achieves this?

choices.text: Use Amazon Macie to scan S3 data for PII, then use the findings to inform AWS Lake Formation column-level or tag-based permissions restricting access to the identified sensitive columns
Use AWS Config alone to both discover and restrict access to PII columns
Use CloudTrail Insights to discover PII patterns in API calls
Rely solely on S3 bucket policies to restrict access to PII, with no cataloging involved

explanation: Macie is designed to discover and classify sensitive data such as PII within S3, and its findings can guide administrators in configuring Lake Formation's fine-grained (column-level or tag-based) permissions to restrict query access to those specific columns in the Data Catalog. AWS Config (B) evaluates resource configuration compliance, not data content, and CloudTrail Insights (C) analyzes API call patterns, not data content.

stem: Which AWS service continuously records and lets you view a timeline of configuration changes to resources such as security groups, S3 bucket policies, and IAM roles, and can evaluate whether resources comply with defined rules?

choices.text: AWS CloudTrail
AWS Config
Amazon Macie
AWS Trusted Advisor

explanation: AWS Config records resource configuration changes over time, provides a configuration timeline, and can evaluate compliance against managed or custom rules, which is distinct from CloudTrail's focus on API call history. CloudTrail (A) logs who made an API call and when but does not model configuration state or compliance the way Config does, and Macie (C) focuses on sensitive data discovery rather than configuration tracking.

stem: A multinational company must ensure that customer data belonging to European Union residents is never stored or processed outside EU AWS Regions, to comply with data sovereignty requirements. Which combination of controls best enforces this at the account/organization level?

choices.text: Rely only on application-level checks in each microservice
Use AWS Organizations service control policies (SCPs) to deny actions that create or use resources outside approved EU Regions, combined with IAM policies and resource tagging for enforcement
Enable CloudTrail logging in all Regions with no preventive controls
Use Amazon Macie to physically move data between Regions automatically

explanation: SCPs applied through AWS Organizations can deny API actions in disallowed Regions across all accounts in scope, providing a preventive, account-level control for data sovereignty, complemented by IAM policies and tagging for granular enforcement. Application-level checks alone (A) can be bypassed or missed, CloudTrail (C) is detective rather than preventive, and Macie (D) does not move or relocate data.

stem: In the Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio governance model, how do project members typically gain governed access to shared data assets like tables and datasets that have been published for reuse across teams?

choices.text: Every project member is granted account-wide IAM administrator access
Members access published data assets through the project's catalog, where subscriptions and permissions to shared assets are governed and scoped to that project
Data assets are copied unencrypted to each member's local machine
There is no concept of shared or catalog assets in SageMaker Unified Studio

explanation: SageMaker Unified Studio lets project members discover and subscribe to published data assets through a governed catalog, where access is scoped to the project and subject to approval and permissions rather than broad account access. Granting administrator access (A) violates least privilege, and the platform does provide a catalog and governance model, ruling out D.

stem: Two business units in the same company, each running its own AWS account, need Business Unit B to run analytical queries against a curated subset of Business Unit A's data lake tables, while Business Unit A retains ownership and control over the underlying data and its permissions. Which pattern best fits this cross-account data governance requirement?

choices.text: Business Unit A exports full table dumps to Business Unit B's S3 bucket weekly

Business Unit A registers its data in AWS Lake Formation and shares specific databases or tables cross-account with Business Unit B's account, which accepts the resource share and grants its own principals access
Business Unit B is given the root credentials of Business Unit A's account
Both accounts are merged into a single AWS account to simplify governance

explanation: Lake Formation supports cross-account data sharing (including via AWS Resource Access Manager) where the owning account registers and grants access to specific catalog resources, and the consuming account accepts the share and manages its own downstream permissions, preserving centralized ownership and governance. Exporting full dumps (A) creates duplicated, unsynchronized data with no centralized governance, and sharing root credentials (C) is a severe security anti-pattern.

stem: A company enabled an AWS Config managed rule to flag any S3 bucket that does not have default encryption enabled, but a newly created noncompliant bucket does not appear as noncompliant in the AWS Config dashboard even after several hours. What is a likely cause the engineer should investigate first?

choices.text: AWS Config evaluates resources only once per year regardless of changes
The AWS Config recorder is not enabled for the S3 resource type in that Region, or the rule's scope excludes the bucket
S3 buckets cannot be evaluated by AWS Config managed rules
The bucket must be manually deleted and recreated for Config to notice it

explanation: If the Config recorder is not tracking the S3 bucket resource type in that Region, or if the rule's scope or trigger settings exclude the new bucket, Config will not evaluate or display its compliance status. AWS Config evaluates far more frequently than annually when configured for configuration-change or periodic triggers, ruling out A, and S3 buckets are a fully supported resource type for AWS Config managed rules, ruling out C.
